extracted.intended_audience: NLP researchers, data scientists, and patent professionals (inventors, patent attorneys) working on patent text analysis and generation
extracted.subtask_description: Survey of NLP tasks, methods, datasets, and evaluation considerations for patent texts, covering summarization, translation, simplification, generation, and innovation recommendation. Emphasizes domain-specific challenges (terminology, legal requirements), dataset/benchmark needs, and LLM usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intrinsic indicators alone insufficient for technology life cycle prediction
rubrics_metrics.description: “using intrinsic indicators from patents as the sole predictor of technology life cycles may not be sufficient.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intrinsic patent signals (classes, citations, etc.) do not capture social needs, user acceptance, market trends, competitive landscape, or strategic decisions. Predictions of life cycle phases should therefore not rely solely on patent-derived indicators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multi-dimensional approach for technology life cycle prediction
rubrics_metrics.description: “a multi-dimensional approach that combines intrinsic patent data with extrinsic information will likely provide a more accurate and holistic prediction of technology life cycles.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine patent-internal features with extrinsic factors (market trends, customer types, company strategy, competitive landscape) to improve accuracy and capture adoption dynamics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent application trend prediction—performance and data limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent application trend prediction aims to predict future patent classification codes for a company given previous filings; reported recall was hardly higher than 20% overall, indicating substantial room for improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat recall (and other predictive metrics) as critical for evaluating methods; recognize company-dependent prediction is a newly proposed task with few datasets and papers—data scarcity and model generalization across companies are major challenges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Innovation recommendations should identify novel R&D opportunities
rubrics_metrics.description: “Innovation recommendations should help companies to identify novel research and development opportunities.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation should focus on usefulness to companies (ability to surface promising, novel directions), not just novelty for its own sake; examples include concept association, gap detection, cross-domain links, and idea generation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal issues around AI-generated inventions (inventorship/ownership)
rubrics_metrics.description: “the use of AI to generate inventions may raise legal issues, notably around inventorship and ownership... The US Patent and Trademark Office, at present, does not consider AI-generated inventions as patentable...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systems that suggest or generate invention ideas must account for evolving legal standards: potential unpatentability of purely AI-generated inventions, inventorship declarations, and risks if AI adds hallucinatory inventive content. These legal constraints limit how generated outputs can be used in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concept association analysis—discover novel combinations of technical concepts
rubrics_metrics.description: Use NLP to identify key concepts in patent documents and analyze associations to discover novel combinations of concepts and suggest potential innovation directions (e.g., identify technologies with technical attributes similar to a target technology).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure ability to find non-trivial, synthesizeable concept pairings; consider injecting controlled randomness (higher temperature) to increase creativity, while monitoring for hallucination or infeasible combos.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technology gap (white-space) detection—find underdeveloped areas
rubrics_metrics.description: Technology gap detection searches for areas within a technology field that are underdeveloped or unexplored using semantic distances (e.g., TechNet).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess robustness to patent-specific terminology and the tendency of patents to form isolated terminological clusters; validate inferred gaps against domain expertise to avoid spurious signals caused by idiosyncratic wording.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-domain analysis—link techniques across fields
rubrics_metrics.description: Cross-domain analysis links patents across different technological fields to find cross-domain techniques that can stimulate breakthrough innovations (e.g., causal extraction with BERT-derived models to output cause–effect matches).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate cross-domain similarity/joining methods on their ability to surface plausible technology–application matches; watch for heavy dependence on differing terminologies across domains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Idea generation with language models—quality and conditioning issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Generative language models can output innovative ideas (e.g., fine-tuned GPT-2 to generate idea titles from keywords) but patent titles are often generic for legal reasons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess idea novelty, specificity, and feasibility rather than headline-level novelty; avoid conditioning on weak inputs (titles or overly generic abstracts) that lead to vacuous outputs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summarization—concise and informative summaries tailored to audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent summarization aims to create concise and informative summaries of patent documents for audiences such as examiners, researchers, engineers, and legal professionals; must extract key aspects like claims, background, and descriptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation should measure informativeness, conciseness, and target-audience appropriateness; summaries may need to preserve legal/technical nuances relevant to downstream tasks (e.g., patent search or analysis).

rubrics_metrics.name: Extractive summarization—preserves wording but may lack coherence or miss implicit info
rubrics_metrics.description: Extractive methods select key phrases or sentences verbatim to retain original context and wording but can be disjointed and may fail to capture information not explicitly stated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use extractive methods when preserving exact wording matters (e.g., legal phrases), but complement them with techniques to ensure coherence and coverage of implicit content; common techniques include TF-IDF and LSA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstractive summarization—more fluent but risks factual distortion and resource intensity
rubrics_metrics.description: Abstractive summarization rephrases source text into shorter outputs that synthesize information; it demands deeper understanding and is more likely to introduce distortions or misrepresent technical/legal terms and is resource-intensive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance fluency with faithfulness: prefer domain-adapted/controlled generation and rigorous factuality checks when using abstractive models for patent texts; transformer-based models have shown strong performance but require care to avoid legal-term drift.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model architecture and long-input capacity matter for patent summarization
rubrics_metrics.description: Transformer-based and long-input models (e.g., PEGASUS, BigBird-PEGASUS, LongT5) outperform LSTM-based models on patent summarization benchmarks; patent descriptions often exceed 10,000 tokens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose architectures and input-length capabilities aligned with patent document sizes; longer context models substantially improve coverage of patent descriptions and performance on benchmarks like BigPatent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for domain-specific evaluation metrics and benchmarks
rubrics_metrics.description: Benchmarks consist of labeled datasets and established metrics (accuracy, precision), but general text evaluation metrics may not be suitable for patent text assessment; many tasks rely on closed-source datasets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop and use labeled, open benchmarks and tailor evaluation metrics to legal/technical fidelity (not only ROUGE/BLEU); encourage patent offices to provide pre-processed datasets to improve reproducibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent translation—terminology precision is crucial (no unacceptable substitutions)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Standard translators tend to vary terms and use synonyms... However, the substitution is not acceptable and can render a patent worthless when it involves features or feature-relevant language.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize terminology fidelity over stylistic variation; control model temperature and adopt domain-specific term glossaries or constrained decoding to avoid harmful substitutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent translation—use domain-specific parallel corpora and pre/post-processing
rubrics_metrics.description: Train translation models on multi-language patent data (e.g., EuroPat, EPO parallel corpora); fix common terminology errors via pre-editing source texts and post-editing outputs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine domain adaptation (fine-tuning on patent parallel corpora) with pre/post-processing to address terminology errors; compare specialized patent MT systems (Patent Translate, WIPO Translate) to general-purpose LLMs for tradeoffs in accuracy vs. fluency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human translators for legal-critical patent translations
rubrics_metrics.description: Machine translations may not always achieve the precision required for legal or formal purposes; consultation with professional human translators is advisable for critical applications (e.g., filings, proceedings).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use automated systems for triage and understanding, but require human review and certification for filings or disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent simplification—retain information while increasing readability
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent simplification aims to translate complex, technical patents into more readable language while ideally retaining all information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design simplification systems to preserve the full meaning and legal scope; use formatting, terminology glossaries, and careful paraphrasing/splitting to increase accessibility without losing critical content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formatting and claim-tree visualization to improve accessibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Macro-level formatting (e.g., claim trees, separating claim features) and micro-level highlighting (nominal terms with references) can increase accessibility without modifying factual content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generate claim dependency graphs and segment claims into preamble/transitional/body to visualize relationships and reduce cognitive load for non-experts; derive discourse references via POS, phrase boundaries, and discourse rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paraphrasing and sentence splitting—trade-off between readability and nuance loss
rubrics_metrics.description: Paraphrasing can rewrite complex sentences into simpler versions via splitting, dropping, and modifying, but may lose subtle nuances and specific terminologies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply controlled paraphrasing with verification steps to ensure no loss of legally relevant meaning; combine rule-based segmentation with statistical/NN paraphrasers and filtering to select appropriate candidates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Controlled simplification attributes (length, lexical/syntactic complexity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicit control tokens for attributes such as length, lexical complexity, and syntactic complexity can tailor simplifications to different audience needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use control-token architectures (e.g., explicit attribute tokens) and tune them for target audiences (technical experts vs. lay readers); lack of in-domain datasets for patents is a limitation to train such models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent writing—legal and linguistic precision, clarity, and formal requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent writing must produce formal, unambiguous, precise language that adheres to legal requirements for grants; automated patent-text generation is difficult because of these constraints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess generated patent sections (claims, descriptions, abstracts) for legal compliance, clarity, precision, and completeness; failures may harm grant prospects or lead to litigation vulnerabilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditioning source selection for patent writing—description-based more promising
rubrics_metrics.description: Title- and abstract-based generation are poorly conditioned (titles are short and abstracts often intentionally vague), whereas description-based claim generation is more promising because descriptions contain detailed embodiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer conditioning generation models on rich description content rather than titles/abstracts; when using abstracts/titles, be aware of limited specificity and the need for substantial downstream revision.

rubrics_metrics.name: LLM-generated claims/specifications require substantial human revision
rubrics_metrics.description: LLMs can improve claim completeness and clarity after fine-tuning, but generated claims often need comprehensive revisions to pass rigorous patent scrutiny; LLMs can introduce ineffective edits that deviate from intended revisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat LLM outputs as drafts requiring expert attorney/agent edits; consider fine-tuning and post-editing pipelines as part of real-world drafting workflows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multi-agent LLM frameworks for patent drafting and analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Multi-LLM agent frameworks (e.g., EvoPat, AutoPatent, PatExpert) can orchestrate planner, writer, examiner, and critique agents to collaborate on complex patent tasks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate agent-based systems for modularity (planning, writing, examining, critiquing), error-handling (critique agents), and adaptability; use human oversight for legal sign-off.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for long-sequence modeling to leverage patent descriptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent descriptions are often very long (far exceed many transformer context lengths); integrating detailed descriptions can significantly improve performance on patent analysis and generation tasks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt long-context models (current LLMs supporting >100k tokens) or hierarchical/efficient long-sequence methods to capture full descriptions and long-range dependencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data and benchmark scarcity—need for labeled patent datasets and open benchmarks
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a lack of labeled patent datasets for many tasks (e.g., novelty prediction, simplification). Benchmarks and shared metrics are essential for fair comparison, but many datasets are closed-source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promote creation and sharing of curated, labeled patent datasets and task-specific benchmarks; design evaluation metrics tailored to patent-specific language and legal requirements.
